messages.body_plain:
Hi Bonnie,

I’m hardly a pro at this, but I like to use the s.class function to plot my PCA results and also to add the legend. It allows better customisation IMO.

For example:

plot.new <http://plot.new>() #clear old plots. pca1 in the next step is the output of the gl.pcoa function

s.class(pca1$scores, pop(your.gl <http://your.gl>), clabel=0, cpoint=2, grid=TRUE, axesell=FALSE, addaxes=TRUE, col=your.colours.cheme) # there are lots of ways of setting your colours. You could just add “col=rainbow”, or you could have previously set a particular colour gradient by e.g.

#  #make a gradient of colours suiting N sites

#load(colorRamps) # a useful package

#NS.col <- colorRamps::blue2red(17) #17 hues on the blue-red spectrum

#then when plotting above you’d add “col=NS.col”

#add a legend

legend(xy.coords(x=c(-10,-3), y=c(0,4)), pch=19, pt.cex=2, bty="n", levels(pop(your.gl <http://your.gl>)), ncol=3, y.intersp=0.5, x.intersp=0.5, col=NS.col,

add.scatter.eig(pca1$eig[1:20],2,1,1, ratio=0.2)#add the scree plot

Good luck.

Olly

Cheers, Bernd

messages.body_plain:
Hi Peco,

Though the conversion gi2gl may work in terms of format, be careful with this.

The reason why silico darts are stored as genind (not genlight) is that it is a haplotype kind of format (ploidy =1) and a conversion into genlight may not be “good”.

Without checking I can see that filters like RepAvg would work, but clearly MAF would not.

I think also PCoA should work. Better to look into the adegenet vignettes for genind object and see what you can do.

A simple

summary(gi)

gives you some summary statistics (might be slow depending on the number of loci).

In principle you can also use the package PopGenReport (but it was meant for maybe max 50 loci and hence it may break especially the pdf version of the package).

Admittedly the support for silicos is lacking currently but that will change in the future (just did not come around to work on it).

Cheers, Bernd

messages.body_plain:
Hi Peco,

dartR does not yet support SilicoDArT analyses. SilicoDArT data comprise presence/absence data for sequence tags (1's and 0's). Essentially they are the same as the null alleles (missing data) in your SNP dataset, except that the SNP dataset is optimized for calling SNPs and the SilicoDArT dataset is optimized for calling presence or absence of the sequence tags.

So, as Bernd has indicated, simply converting your genind object (containing the SilicoDArT data) to a genlight object is unlikely to be terribly reliable for all but a few analyses.

What we need is for someone with a deep interest in SilicoDArT to write scripts for incorporation into dartR. It probably won't happen at our end until we have a project that demands them. A little challenge for you perhaps :)

All the best,

A

messages.body_plain:
Hi James,

Half the answer is:

The loci names are not returned but their number in the order of your genlight object, so for example you can do:

> ldf <- gl.report.ld(possums.gl <http://possums.gl>)

Start to calculate LD for all pairs of loci...

Using 1 cores in 2  chunks.

Depending on the number of loci this may take a while...

nchunks specifies the number of steps in the progress bar and the number of intermediate saves, but slows the computation a bit. nchunks = 1 is fastest.

Seperate all 300 loci...

Generate all possible pairs: 19900 ...

Calculate LD for all pairs...

# Simulations: 19900 . Took 13 seconds.

Results are saved as object LDallp under LDallp.rdata.

Once you have checked you can delete your LD_chunks_  files.

> ldf$loc1name <- locNames(possums.gl <http://possums.gl>)[ldf$loc1]

> ldf$loc2name <- locNames(possums.gl <http://possums.gl>)[ldf$loc2]

The last two lines add the names of the loci to the output data frame.

In terms of filtering we do not have a function yet, but happy to write one. It is a bit “tricky” and will not happen in the next 2 weeks.

The reason why a bit more involved is because the r2 value (if used as a threshold) is for pairs of loci and you basically have to decide which of the two you want to “kick” out (obviously you can also simply kick out both) but if you want to keep most loci then a stepwise approach is smarter.

As an example think about you have 3 loci, so three pairwise comparison  1-2, 1-3 and 2-3. Assuming 1-2 and 2-3 are in ld and you want to kick them out, then by kicking out loci of both pairs all loci are gone. If you instead kick out loci 2 and 1-3 are not linked then you would have two loci left to work with. So such a filter is more efficient than just simply using the threshold for all pairs at once.

In case you are versatile in R and want to write it yourself please send me the script.

Cheers, Bernd

In case you are fine to kick out all loci pairs you can use

> index <- ldf$R2>0.1
> table(index)

index
FALSE  TRUE
19178   722

So 722 pairs are higher than 0.1 (my chosen threshold, this is a simulated data set so I would not expect any high R2)

barplot(table(c(ldf$loc1name[index], ldf$loc2name[index])), las=2)

So a smart approach would be now to get rid of loci 160 (is 32 times linked with another loci) and then check again the pairs remove the one with most lds and so on).

Hi Bonnie and Andrzej,

Just an alternate approach to those already given.

dartR was written for input and exploratory analysis, and we were keen not to fall into the trap of duplicating functions that were already available in R.

So my advice would be to grab the associated data important for your plotting

indNames(gl)
popNames(gl)

and the coordinates of the points

pcoa <- gl.pcoa(gl,nfactors=2)
pcoa$scores

bundle them into a dataframe

df <- data.frame(id=indNames(gl),pop=popNames(gl),pcoa$scores)

and then use ggplot or any R plotting packages you are familiar with to produce the plots you require.

Might be some minor syntax errors in the above, as I am not close to a computer.

Arthur
